en:
【Jian Chuan, Chapter 37】

Why does the mourning garment for three years use coarse hemp? Coarse hemp is an ugly appearance, used to express the inner sorrow outwardly. The mourner for three years looks like coarse hemp; for one year, like flax; for nine months, like one who is still; for five months and three months, the appearance may be normal. This is sorrow manifested in appearance and body.
The weeping for three years' mourning is like going and not returning; for one year's mourning, like going and returning; for nine months' mourning, it is winding and prolonged; for five months and three months, a sorrowful countenance suffices. This is sorrow manifested in voice and sound.
For three years' mourning, one only responds with "yes" but does not converse; for one year's mourning, one converses but does not speak at length; for nine months' mourning, one speaks but does not discuss; for five months and three months, one discusses but does not reach the point of joy. This is sorrow manifested in speech and language.
For three years' mourning, one fasts for three days; for one year's mourning, for two days; for nine months' mourning, for three meals; for five months and three months, for two meals; for a scholar-official who participates in the encoffining, one meal is skipped. Therefore, for the mourning of parents, after the encoffining, one drinks porridge, eating a handful of rice in the morning and a handful in the evening; for one year's mourning, one eats coarse food and drinks water, not eating vegetables or fruits; for nine months' mourning, one does not eat vinegar or sauces; for five months and three months, one does not drink sweet wine. This is sorrow manifested in food and drink.
For the mourning of parents, after the sacrifice of repose and the cessation of weeping, one eats coarse food and drinks water, not eating vegetables or fruits; after one year at the Lesser Repast, one eats vegetables and fruits; after another year at the Greater Repast, one has vinegar and sauces; after the intervening month at the final sacrifice, one drinks sweet wine. When first drinking wine, one first drinks sweet wine. When first eating meat, one first eats dried meat.
For the mourning of parents, one dwells in a lean-to hut, sleeps on straw with a clod of earth as a pillow, and does not remove the mourning sash or headband; for one year's mourning, one dwells in a whitewashed room, with a mat of rushes cut but not sewn; for nine months' mourning, one sleeps on a mat; for five months and three months, a bed is permissible. This is sorrow manifested in dwelling and resting.
For the mourning of parents, after the sacrifice of repose and the cessation of weeping, one props up the ridgepole, trims the screen, and uses a rush mat cut but not sewn; after one year at the Lesser Repast, one dwells in a whitewashed room and sleeps on a mat; after another year at the Greater Repast, one returns to the regular sleeping quarters; after the intervening month at the final sacrifice, one uses a bed.
……

Young Master:
Your bro is back to share some more fun! Coincidentally, as soon as I entered Kaifeng City, I received an invitation. Apparently, the imperial dogs organized a "Barking Brigade Year-End Summary Meeting," and any passing dog could join in.
And guess what I found when I got there?
Amidst the sea of dogs, I actually met a big yellow dog with the exact same name as mine!
The other guy works for a wanderer from Qinghe, someone called... $C$L#Y$PN#E$C or something. I've never heard of them, but with your vast knowledge of the Jianghu, maybe you have.
That dog was bragging about how great his master is, calling them the "Number One Poop Scooper of Qinghe" and "Number One Dog-Brother Treater"... It really ticked me off. Wasn't he clearly insulting you? You are the true Number One of Qinghe!
I barked back at him on the spot. That Fulu Erwa wouldn't back down, barking, "Our Young Master can stand still for three days and nights, can yours? Our Young Master can build houses in an instant, can yours? Our Young Master can change clothes seven or eight times a day, can yours?"
Don't worry, your brother didn't let you down. I said, "Our Young Master can do more than just that..." I'll stop here, they're calling for silence, the meeting is starting. I'll tell you the rest later.
Your most reliable Fu Luwa

扑朔篇

从前有个叫赵七的猎户，在雪中猎了只肥兔，那兔子毛色油亮，重逾寻常。
赵七心下欢喜，遂将它剥皮烹肉，以飨三五友人。
众人品尝后，都赞不绝口，称其油脂丰腴犹胜羔羊，赵七因此颇为得意。
谁知夜半时分，寒月照梁，庖厨竟生异响，似有兽崽哀啼。
赵七提灯前往，但见灶台旁赫然出现数个血爪印，悬于梁上的兔皮也鼓动不止，如在呼吸。

三日后，赵七腹胀如鼓，疼痛难忍，于是四下求医，却无人能治。
秦川一巫医听闻此事，断言道：“孕兽怀三魂，君腹中恐结怨胎。”
赵七此症，乃是食了有孕的雌兔所致。

果不其然，在巫医的帮助下，赵七呕出一团绒毛，像极了初生的幼兔。
打那之后，秦川的猎户们便定下一条规矩，名为“三不杀”。
——孕兽不杀，拜月不杀，穴中有雏不杀。
en:
The Tale of the Mysterious Hunt

Once, a hunter named Zhao Qi caught a fat rabbit in the snow. Its fur gleamed, and it felt heavier than most.
Pleased with his prize, Zhao Qi skinned it and cooked it up for a few friends. Everyone praised the meat, saying its rich fat rivaled even lamb. Zhao Qi swelled with pride.
But that night, under the cold moon, strange sounds crept from the kitchen, like the cries of a newborn beast. Zhao Qi lit a lantern, only to find claw marks lay smeared in blood by the stove. The rabbit's skin, hung from the beam, seemed to rise and fall softly, as if it were still breathing.

Three days later, Zhao Qi's belly swelled with pain. No physician could cure him.
A shaman from Qinchuan heard of his plight and suggested, "A pregnant beast carries three souls. You've taken its life, now a vengeful spirit grows inside you."

With the shaman's help, Zhao Qi finally vomited a hairy mass, shaped like a newborn rabbit.
From that day on, hunters in Qinchuan followed a rule they called the Three Rules of the Hunt:
Do not kill a pregnant beast, do not hunt on moonlit nights, and do not disturb a den with cubs inside.

zh:
昔有樵者，闻不见山中有藏珍之鸟，遂往求之。
及山穷水尽处，果见宝石累累，有二鸟栖于侧，一鸦一燕，竟作人语。
燕问于鸦：“此物非糜非谷，守之何益？”
鸦答：“欲赠予天下人，使人再无贫富之别，尽居琼瑶之室，尽衣云锦之裳。”
燕又问：“善矣！曷辍而不为？”
鸦喟然：“昔众鸟衔石出山，贫者见之，竞相争夺，自戕骨肉；富者见衔石之禽，网罗弋射，笼而戏之。”
二鸟皆默然。未几，燕复语：“既知其不可为，何故教我闻之？”
鸦答：“怀璧者罪，当藏以待时。子春去而秋来，得一信字，不辞风雨之劳，得一恒字。守信而心恒，故以相托。”
燕问：“世人只知君怀宝自珍，却不知俟时而出之理。身劳名损，却受世人之讥，君亦甘受乎？”
鸦振翅昂首，应曰：“人言鸦即墨者，既为墨者，但存此心，何计毁誉？人心不足，墨者喂之。人求米面，墨者铸铁犁造木牛，以养天下；人求酒肉，墨者酿美酒养肥豕，以飨众生。”
闻此，樵夫惊异，踉跄归告。
翌日率邻再往，惟见空谷寂寂，鸟鸣上下，宝石灵禽，俱化云烟矣。
en:
Once there was a woodcutter who heard that deep in the mountains there lived birds that kept hidden treasure, and so he went looking for them.
At the far end of the mountain, where there was nowhere left to go, he came upon heaps of gemstones. Beside them perched two birds, one a raven and one a swallow, and to his astonishment they spoke in human voices.
Swallow asked Raven, "This is neither fodder nor grain. What good is there in guarding it?"
Raven replied, "I would give it to all people under Heaven, so there would be no more divide between rich and poor, so all might live in halls of jade and wear robes of cloud-brocade."
Swallow asked again, "A worthy thought. Why then stop short of it?"
Raven sighed. "In the past, when the birds carried stones out of the mountains, the poor fought to seize them, even turning on their own kin. The rich, seeing birds that bore such stones, cast nets and loosed arrows, caging them for sport."
At this, both birds fell silent. After a while, Swallow spoke again. "If you know it cannot be done, why tell me of it?"
Raven answered, "To carry jade is to invite trouble. Better to hide it and wait for the right time. You leave in spring and return in autumn, and so have earned trust. You do not shrink from wind and rain, and so have earned constancy. Because you keep faith and remain steadfast, I entrust this to you."
Swallow said, "People know only that you keep your treasure to yourself. They do not know that you are waiting for the right time to bring it forth. Your body is worn down, your name diminished, and still the world mocks you. Do you truly accept this?"
Raven spread its wings and lifted its head. "People say Raven is a Mohist. And if one truly walks the Mohist path, what need is there to care for praise or blame? What the human heart wants, the Mohists provide. If people want grain, we forge plows and build wooden oxen to feed the world. If people want wine, we brew fine spirits; if they want meat, we raise fat hogs to nourish all living things."
Hearing this, the woodcutter was astonished and hurried home to tell the tale.
The next day he returned with his neighbors, but found only an empty valley, hushed and still, with birdsong rising and falling above. The gemstones and the wondrous birds were both gone, vanished like smoke.

zh:
《说文解字》有云：“驳，马色不纯。从马，爻声。”西南矮脚中杂而不纯者，为赤驳。
《华阳国志·南中志》记载：“长老传言，滇池有神马，或交焉，即生骏驹，俗称称之曰‘滇池驹’，日行五百里。”唐宋时期，《蛮书》又云：“马出越赕山东面一带……尾高，尤善驰骤，日行数百里。……腾冲及申赕亦出马，次赕，滇池尤佳。”《新唐书·南诏传》亦载：“越赕之西有荐草，产善马，世称‘越赕骏’。始生若羔，岁中，细莎縻之，饮以米渖，七年可御，日驰数百里。”滇马即为矮脚马，因产于滇池，故名“西南矮脚”。
西南矮脚体格极小，四肢较细，颈短头直，眼大额广，蹄小而质坚，以耐力见长，乘、挽、驮均可，为西南最常见的马种。
en:
The Shuowen Jiezi explains: "The character bo means a horse of impure color." Among the Southwestern Ponies, those with such an uneven, mixed red coat are called Chibo.
Legends from the Huayang Chorography tell of a divine steed that once rose from Dianchi Lake. Its offspring, known as "Dianchi Foals," were said to travel five hundred li a day. Later, during the Tang and Song dynasties, texts like the Book of the Man and the New Book of Tang praised the swift, high-tailed horses bred on the lush grasslands of the region, famed as "Yuetan Steeds." These Dian Horses, named for their origin near Dianchi Lake, are also known as Southwestern Ponies.
Small in stature, they have fine limbs, a short neck, a broad forehead, and firm, compact hooves. Prized for their endurance, they are suited for riding, pulling, and carrying loads, making them the most common breed in the southwest.

【梁惠王章句·下】

孟子对曰：仲尼之徒，无道桓、文之事者，是以后世无传焉。臣未之闻也。无以，则王乎？
曰：德何如则可以王矣？
曰：保民而王，莫之能御也。
曰：若寡人者，可以保民乎哉？曰：可。曰：何由知吾可也？
曰：臣闻之胡龁曰：王坐于堂上，有牵牛而过堂下者，王见之，曰：牛何之？对曰：将以衅钟。王曰：舍之，吾不忍其觳觫，若无罪而就死地。对曰：然则废衅钟与？曰：何可废也？以羊易之。不识有诸？曰：有之。
曰：是心足以王矣。百姓皆以王为爱也，臣固知王之不忍也。
王曰：然。诚有百姓者，齐国虽褊小，吾何爱一牛？即不忍其觳觫，若无罪而就死地，故以羊易之也。
曰：王无异于百姓之以王为爱也。以小易大，彼恶知之？王若隐其无罪而就死地，则牛羊何择焉？
王笑曰：是诚何心哉！我非爱其财而易之以羊也，宜乎百姓之谓我爱也。
曰：“无伤也，是乃仁术也，见牛未见羊也。君子之于禽兽也，见其生不忍见其死，闻其声不忍食其肉，是以君子远庖厨也。
王说，曰：诗云：他人有心，予忖度之，夫子之谓也。夫我乃行之，反而求之，不得吾心。夫子言之，于我心有戚戚焉。此心之所以合于王者，何也？
曰：有复于王者，曰：吾力足以举百钧，而不足以举一羽，明足以察秋豪之末，而不见舆薪。则王许之乎？曰：否。
今恩足以及禽兽，而功不至于百姓者，独何与？然则一羽之不举，为不用力焉；舆薪之不见，为不用明焉；百姓之不见保，为不用恩焉。故王之不王，不为也，非不能也。
曰：不为者与不能者之形何以异？
曰：挟大山以超北海，语人曰：我不能。是诚不能也。为长者折枝，语人曰：我不能。是不为也，非不能也。故王之不王，非挟大山以超北海之类也；王之不王，是折枝之类也。
老吾老，以及人之老；幼吾幼，以及人之幼，天下可运于掌。诗云：刑于寡妻，至于兄弟，以御于家邦。言举斯心加诸彼而已，故推恩足以保四海，不推恩无以保妻子。古之人所以大过人者，无他焉，善推其所为而已矣。
今恩足以及禽兽，而功不至于百姓者，独何与？
权，然后知轻重；度，然后知长短。物皆然，心为甚。王请度之。
抑王兴甲兵，危士臣，搆怨于诸侯，然后快于心与？
王曰：否。吾何快于是？将以求吾所大欲也。
曰：王之所大欲，可得闻与？王笑而不言。
曰：为肥甘不足于口与？轻暖不足于体与？抑为采色不足视于目与？声音不足听于耳与？便嬖不足使令于前与？王之诸臣皆足以供之，而王岂为是哉？曰：否，吾不为是也。
曰：然则王之所大欲可知已。欲辟土地，朝秦、楚，莅中国而抚四夷也。以若所为，求若所欲，犹缘木而求鱼也。王曰：若是其甚与？
曰：殆有甚焉。缘木求鱼，虽不得鱼，无后灾。以若所为，求若所欲，尽心力而为之，后必有灾。曰：可得闻与？
曰：邹人与楚人战，则王以为孰胜？曰：楚人胜。
曰：然则小固不可以敌大，寡固不可以敌众，弱固不可以敌强。海内之地，方千里者九，齐集有其一，以一服八，何以异于邹敌楚哉？盖亦反其本矣。
今王发政施仁，使天下仕者皆欲立于王之朝，耕者皆欲耕于王之野，商贾皆欲藏于王之市，行旅皆欲出于王之涂，天下之欲疾其君者皆欲赴诉于王。其若是，孰能御之？
王曰：吾惛，不能进于是矣，愿夫子辅吾志，明以教我。我虽不敏，请尝试之。
曰：无恒产而有恒心者，惟士为能。若民则无恒产，因无恒心。苟无恒心，放辟邪侈，无不为已。及陷于罪，然后从而刑之，是罔民也。焉有仁人在位，罔民而可为也？是故明君制民之产，必使仰足以事父母，俯足以畜妻子，乐岁终身饱，凶年免于死亡，然后驱而之善，故民之从之也轻。
今也制民之产，仰不足以事父母，俯不足以畜妻子，乐岁终身苦，凶年不免于死亡。此惟救死而恐不赡，奚暇治礼义哉？
王欲行之，则盍反其本矣。
五亩之宅，树之以桑，五十者可以衣帛矣。鸡豚狗彘之畜，无失其时，七十者可以食肉矣。百亩之田，勿夺其时，八口之家可以无饥矣。谨庠序之教，申之以孝悌之义，颁白者不负戴于道路矣。老者衣帛食肉，黎民不饥不寒，然而不王者，未之有也。
en:
[Part of King Hui of Liang: II]

Mencius replied, "There were none of the disciples of Zhongni who spoke about the affairs of Huan and Wen, and therefore they have not been transmitted to these after-ages—your servant has not heard them. If you will have me speak, let it be about royal government."
The king said, "What virtue must there be in order to attain to royal sway?"
Mencius answered, "The love and protection of the people; with this there is no power which can prevent a ruler from attaining to it."
The king asked again, "Is such an one as I competent to love and protect the people?" Mencius said, "Yes." "How do you know that I am competent for that?"
I heard the following incident from Hu He: "The king," said he, "was sitting aloft in the hall, when a person appeared, leading an ox past the lower part of it. The king saw him, and asked, 'Where is the ox going?' The person replied, 'We are going to consecrate a bell with its blood.' The king said, 'Let it go. I cannot bear its frightened appearance, as if it were an innocent person going to the place of death.' The person answered, 'Shall we then omit the consecration of the bell?' The king said, 'How can that be omitted? Change it for a sheep.'" I do not know whether this incident really occurred.
The king replied, "It did," and then Mencius said, "The heart seen in this is sufficient to carry you to the royal sway. The people all supposed that your Majesty grudged the animal, but your servant knows surely, that it was your Majesty's not being able to bear the sight, which made you do as you did."
The king said, "You are right. And yet there really was an appearance of what the people condemned. But though Qi be a small and narrow State, how should I grudge one ox! Indeed it was because I could not bear its frightened appearance, as if it were an innocent person going to the place of death, that therefore I changed it for a sheep."
Mencius pursued, "Let not your Majesty deem it strange that the people should think you were grudging the animal. When you changed a large one for a small, how should they know the true reason? If you felt pained by its being led without guilt to the place of death, what was there to choose between an ox and a sheep?"
The king laughed and said, "What really was my mind in the matter! I did not grudge the expense of it, and changed it for a sheep! There was reason in the people's saying that I grudged it."
"There is no harm in their saying so," said Mencius. "Your conduct was an artifice of benevolence. You saw the ox, and had not seen the sheep. So is the superior person affected towards animals, that, having seen them alive, one cannot bear to see them die; having heard their dying cries, one cannot bear to eat their flesh. Therefore one keeps away from one's slaughter-house and cook-room."
The king was pleased, and said, "It is said in the Book of Poetry, 'The minds of others, I am able by reflection to measure;' this is verified, my Master, in your discovery of my motive. I indeed did the thing, but when I turned my thoughts inward, and examined into it, I could not discover my own mind. When you, Master, spoke those words, the movements of compassion began to work in my mind. How is it that this heart has in it what is equal to the royal sway?"
Mencius replied, "Suppose a person were to make this statement to your Majesty:—'My strength is sufficient to lift three thousand catties, but it is not sufficient to lift one feather; my eyesight is sharp enough to examine the point of an autumn hair, but I do not see a waggon-load of faggots;' would your Majesty allow what he said?" "No," was the answer, on which Mencius proceeded,
"'Now here is kindness sufficient to reach to animals, and no benefits are extended from it to the people—How is this? Is an exception to be made here? The truth is, the feather is not lifted, because strength is not used; the waggon-load of firewood is not seen, because the eyesight is not used; and the people are not loved and protected, because kindness is not employed. Therefore your Majesty's not exercising the royal sway, is because you do not do it, not because you are not able to do it."
The king asked, "How may the difference between the not doing a thing, and the not being able to do it, be represented?"
Mencius replied, "In such a thing as taking the Tai mountain under your arm, and leaping over the north sea with it, if you say to people—'I am not able to do it,' that is a real case of not being able. In such a matter as breaking off a branch from a tree at the order of a superior, if you say to people—'I am not able to do it,' that is a case of not doing it, it is not a case of not being able to do it. Therefore your Majesty's not exercising the royal sway, is not such a case as that of taking the Tai mountain under your arm, and leaping over the north sea with it. Your Majesty's not exercising the royal sway is a case like that of breaking off a branch from a tree."
"Treat with the reverence due to age the elders in your own family, so that the elders in the families of others shall be similarly treated; treat with the kindness due to youth the young in your own family, so that the young in the families of others shall be similarly treated—do this, and the kingdom may be made to go round in your palm. It is said in the Book of Poetry, 'His example affected his wife. It reached to his brothers, and his family of the State was governed by it.'—The language shows how King Wen simply took his kindly heart, and exercised it towards those parties. Therefore the carrying out his kindness of heart by a prince will suffice for the love and protection of all within the four seas, and if he do not carry it out, he will not be able to protect his wife and children. The way in which the ancients came greatly to surpass other people, was no other but this:—simply that they knew well how to carry out, so as to affect others, what they themselves did."
Now your kindness is sufficient to reach to animals and no benefits are extended from it to reach the people. How is this? Is an exception to be made here?
"By weighing, we know what things are light, and what heavy. By measuring, we know what things are long, and what short. The relations of all things may be thus determined, and it is of the greatest importance to estimate the motions of the mind. I beg your Majesty to measure it."
"You collect your equipments of war, endanger your soldiers and officers, and excite the resentment of the other princes—do these things cause you pleasure in your mind?"
The king replied, "No. How should I derive pleasure from these things? My object in them is to seek for what I greatly desire."
Mencius said, "May I hear from you what it is that you greatly desire?" The king laughed and did not speak.
Mencius resumed, "Are you led to desire it, because you have not enough of rich and sweet food for your mouth? Or because you have not enough of light and warm clothing for your body? Or because you have not enough of beautifully coloured objects to delight your eyes? Or because you have not voices and tones enough to please your ears? Or because you have not enough of attendants and favourites to stand before you and receive your orders? Your Majesty's various officers are sufficient to supply you with those things. How can your Majesty be led to entertain such a desire on account of them?" "No," said the king; "my desire is not on account of them."
Mencius added, "Then, what your Majesty greatly desires may be known. You wish to enlarge your territories, to have Qin and Chu wait at your court, to rule the Middle Kingdom, and to attract to you the barbarous tribes that surround it. But doing what you do to seek for what you desire is like climbing a tree to seek for fish." The king said, "Is it so bad as that?"
"It is even worse," was the reply. "If you climb a tree to seek for fish, although you do not get the fish, you will not suffer any subsequent calamity. But doing what you do to seek for what you desire, doing it moreover with all your heart, you will assuredly afterwards meet with calamities." The king asked, "May I hear from you the proof of that?"
Mencius said, "If the people of Zou should fight with the people of Chu, which of them does your Majesty think would conquer?" "The people of Chu would conquer."
"Yes; and so it is certain that a small country cannot contend with a great, that few cannot contend with many, that the weak cannot contend with the strong. The territory within the four seas embraces nine divisions, each of a thousand li square. All Qi together is but one of them. If, with one part you try to subdue the other eight, what is the difference between that and Zou's contending with Chu? For, with such a desire, you must turn back to the proper course for its attainment."
"Now, if your Majesty will institute a government whose action shall be benevolent, this will cause all the officers in the kingdom to wish to stand in your Majesty's court, and all the farmers to wish to plough in your Majesty's fields, and all the merchants, both travelling and stationary, to wish to store their goods in your Majesty's market-places, and all travelling strangers to wish to make their tours on your Majesty's roads, and all throughout the kingdom who feel aggrieved by their rulers to wish to come and complain to your Majesty. And when they are so bent, who will be able to keep them back?"
The king said, "I am stupid, and not able to advance to this. I wish you, my Master, to assist my intentions. Teach me clearly; although I am deficient in intelligence and vigour, I will essay and try to carry your instructions into effect."
Mencius replied, "They are only people of education, who, without a certain livelihood, are able to maintain a fixed heart. As to the people, if they have not a certain livelihood, it follows that they will not have a fixed heart. And if they have not a fixed heart, there is nothing which they will not do, in the way of self-abandonment, of moral deflection, of depravity, and of wild license. When they thus have been involved in crime, to follow them up and punish them—this is to entrap the people. How can such a thing as entrapping the people be done under the rule of a benevolent person? Therefore an intelligent ruler will regulate the livelihood of the people, so as to make sure that, for those above them, they shall have sufficient wherewith to serve their parents, and, for those below them, sufficient wherewith to support their wives and children; that in good years they shall always be abundantly satisfied, and that in bad years they shall escape the danger of perishing. After this he may urge them, and they will proceed to what is good, for in this case the people will follow after it with ease."
"Now, the livelihood of the people is so regulated, that, above, they have not sufficient wherewith to serve their parents, and, below, they have not sufficient wherewith to support their wives and children. Notwithstanding good years, their lives are continually embittered, and, in bad years, they do not escape perishing. In such circumstances they only try to save themselves from death, and are afraid they will not succeed. What leisure have they to cultivate propriety and righteousness?"
"If your Majesty wishes to effect this regulation of the livelihood of the people, why not turn to that which is the essential step to it?"
"Let mulberry-trees be planted about the homesteads with their five mu, and persons of fifty years may be clothed with silk. In keeping fowls, pigs, dogs, and swine, let not their times of breeding be neglected, and persons of seventy years may eat flesh. Let there not be taken away the time that is proper for the cultivation of the farm with its hundred mu, and the family of eight mouths that is supported by it shall not suffer from hunger. Let careful attention be paid to education in schools, the inculcation in it especially of the filial and congenial duties, and grey-haired men will not be seen upon the roads, carrying burdens on their backs or on their heads. It never has been that the ruler of a State where such results were seen—the old wearing silk and eating flesh, and the black-haired people suffering neither from hunger nor cold—did not attain to the royal dignity."
All better now... That awful feeling's finally gone...

吉梦维何，维熊维罴。

熊在古代被视为吉祥的象征，是古人对儿孙满堂的期望。宋代流行一种撒帐钱的习俗，旧时婚礼，待夫妻交拜完毕，并坐床沿，此时新娘抛洒通宝以表祝福。这种通宝上刻印的文字，便是维熊维罴，多子多孙这样的吉祥话。
en:
What dreams are truly auspicious? Those of bears, both great and small. 

In ancient times, bears were seen as symbols of good fortune, representing hopes for a large and prosperous family. During the Song Dynasty, there was a wedding custom known as "scattering bridal coins." After the couple completed their ceremonial bows and sat on the edge of the bed, the bride would toss bronze coins as a gesture of blessing. These coins were often engraved with phrases like "bears and grizzlies," or "many sons and grandsons," a traditional wish for fortune and fertility.

zh:
少年望着那烟火缭绕的千级长阶，再一次重重地磕下红肿的额头。
故乡大疫，众人药石无医。他孤身一人跋涉百里，只为了到那香火最鼎盛的道观，为爷娘父老求点什么。
符水、丹药、咒箓，只要能救人，什么都好。
他迈着早已麻木的双腿，咬紧牙关，一步一叩首。泪已流干，血已结痂。可他无法停下。他知道，长阶尽头是可以拯救家乡的希望。哪怕这希望只有千万分之一。
一步一步，日落西沉。他的眼前出现了幻影，耳鸣声像尖刃一般在脑海中搅起剧痛。 最终，少年无力地躺在了山门前。眼前，只剩一缕清辉。

冰轮宫的小道士打着哈欠走出山门，发现了昏倒的求药少年。
等少年醒来，他已经躺在了净素的房间中。
他拥有了新的名字，也知晓了那不敢思索的结局——瘟疫比少年的双腿更快，家乡已无复人烟。
那一天，冰轮宫的钟声格外沉重，少年干哑的哭号如同泣血的寒鸦。
en:
The boy gazed at the thousand-step staircase wreathed in incense smoke and once again knocked his already red and swollen forehead heavily against the ground. 
A great plague had struck his homeland; no medicine could cure it. He had trekked a hundred miles alone just to reach the most popular Daoist temple, to beg for something—anything—for his parents and elders. 
Talisman water, elixirs, spell scrolls... anything that could save people would do. 
Moving on long-numbed legs, gritting his teeth, he bowed with every step. His tears had dried, his blood had scabbed. But he couldn't stop. He knew that at the end of the long staircase lay the hope that could save his hometown, even if that hope was one in a million. 
Step by step, the sun sank in the west. Hallucinations appeared before his eyes; the ringing in his ears stabbed through his mind like a sharp blade, stirring up agony. Finally, the boy collapsed powerlessly before the mountain gate. Before his eyes, only a wisp of clear light remained. 
A young Ice Wheel Palace acolyte, yawning, emerged from the gate and found the unconscious boy who had come seeking medicine. 
When the boy awoke, he was lying in a plain, clean room. 
He received a new name and learned the ending he hadn't dared to contemplate—the plague had been faster than the boy's legs. His homeland was no more, its people gone. 
That day, the Ice Wheel Palace's bell tolled with unusual heaviness. The boy's hoarse wails were like the cry of a blood-weeping crow in the cold.

This morning, I was shocked when I got to the medicine hut, there was a whole crowd of people!

Did you get that strange sect letter too? The one with entries dated days into the future? I went straight to Master Jiang to ask about it, and his face changed on the spot. He tried to play it cool, said, "This matter will be thoroughly investigated," and then shuffled off like his legs were failing.

It's the first time I've ever seen him like that. Ha! He's always the one catching our mistakes, so it's nice to finally catch him slipping.

Naturally, I took the chance to ask for more than just #Ygetting back the sect points they wrongly docked#E. I squeezed a bit more out of him. Some #YEcho Jades#E surely aren't enough; I made sure you got some #YReputation#E too.

I know you've had your eye on our disciple robes for a while. Have you managed to trade for one yet? If not, I hope this helps you get there soon. If you have already, no worries! Between us, I heard the Qianjin Hall is working on some new designs. You just might find something you like even more.

Alright, I won't keep you any longer. I know how busy a Silver Needle disciple is, every incense stick's delay could cost dozens of patients! Don't forget to claim the goodies I sent with this letter~

年轻人：
       好久不见，最近过得还好吗？
       托你的福，摊子的生意很好。你阿婶她很久没有这么高兴了，每天笑盈盈地和来往客人唠家常，开心的时候还会借着琵琶摊小娘子的曲子跳上几步！不忙的时候，老张和老幺还张罗着去和赛神队的几个小伙子比赛，哈哈。
      天水集的大伙儿都会提起你，说你行侠仗义，我们听着都很开心，也惦记着你。你阿婶怕你在外面吃不饱穿不暖，时常念叨你呢。有时间就来摊子坐坐啊。
      对了，开烫菜摊子赚了些钱，我们想着也帮衬帮衬别人，就做了些饭菜送给了几个老伙计。怕他们觉得不好意思，我们几个就说，是你要给他们送的。他们还奇怪，说怎么会有没见过的好心人惦记他们呢。老张说这孩子就是这样的，是个热心肠的大侠！他们不太好意思，就给你写了字条，你一起看看吧。
      好了，不说了，待会要来客人了，就到这儿吧。
      希望你一个人在外吃饱穿暖，平平安安。
<IMAGE id='im1' image_url='https://h72.fp.ps.netease.com/file/6891d8b0fd5195a8648cba21bX9dRyBU06' size='2290*1296' color='255;255;255')'></IMAGE>
en:
Young Hero: 
Long time no see. How have you been? 
Thanks to you, the stall is doing great. Your Auntie hasn't been this happy in ages—she smiles, chatting with customers all day, and even dances a few steps when the Pipa lady plays! When it's slow, Old Zhang and Old Yao even try to race the lads from the deity competition team, haha. 
Everyone at Skybrim Market speaks of your chivalry. We are happy to hear it and miss you often. Your Auntie worries you aren't eating well or staying warm. She talks about you all the time. Come visit the stall when you can. 
Oh, we made some money from the scalding vegetable stall, so we thought we'd help others out. We sent some food to a few old partners. We were afraid they'd feel embarrassed, so we said it was from you. They were surprised a kind hero remembered them! Old Zhang said, "That child is just warm-hearted like that!" They were shy, so they wrote you notes. Take a look. 
Okay, customers are coming. I'll stop here. 
Stay warm, fed, and safe out there.

泾渭合流之处，水面辽阔，如薮如渊。此地曾有城寨，遍植夭桃，落英缤纷，盛开时花满江汀，如胭脂浮萍，乃天下绝景。人称此地为桃林塞。 
桃林塞西临秦川，东望长安，乃长安西门户。凡自秦川入长安者莫不经此，检验通牒，验明身货后方可向东行。
有窃国者，为取天下至宝，封湖闭塞。众多武林中人困于塞中。后城塞崩毁，死伤无数。绝色风景已成绝唱，英雄豪杰尸骨无存。
余临此地，但觉清风徐来，唯见天水一色。
嗟乎！生前名声噪，死后一萍草。天地悠悠，浮生如芥，踽踽凭湖，吾谁与言？
en:
Where the two rivers meet, the waters stretch wide and still, vast as a lake and deep as an abyss. Once, a fortress stood here, surrounded by thriving peach trees. When they blossomed, petals fluttered like delicate blush-colored drifts, blanketing the riverbanks and floating atop the water like a living tapestry, a spectacle unrivaled under heaven. This place was known as Peachgrove Pass.
To the west, Peachgrove Pass bordered Qinchuan; to the east, it gazed toward Chang'an, serving as the city's western gateway. All who entered Chang'an from Qinchuan passed through here, their identities and goods carefully examined before they were allowed to continue east.
Yet, in time, a ruthless usurper, driven by hunger for the nation's greatest treasures, sealed the lake and choked the rivers. Countless wanderers found themselves trapped within the pass. Then came the collapse, and with it countless lives lost. That breathtaking scene was destroyed forever, and the heroes who once walked these grounds were laid to rest, their bones scattered and forgotten.
When I arrive, only the gentle breeze greets me, and the eye meets nothing but water blending into sky.
Ah, how fleeting fame is. Bright in life, yet in death no more than a lone petal drifting on the water. The world stretches vast and eternal; life is no more than a speck of dust. Standing alone by the lake, I have no one to speak to.

Dumpling came from a big family, and every single one of them was remarkable.
One was a master of mimicry, another could scale any wall. One was a genius at finding food, and another had the courage to wander the world alone.
And then there was Dumpling. What was his talent? He couldn't quite say. He often felt a little out of place in such a talented crowd.
His one true skill, perhaps, was his ability to curl himself into a perfect, fluffy white ball, round and soft. He never said it out loud, but it weighed on him.
Then, he found the Spiritroost Crag. No one here expected anything of him. No one compared him to his siblings.
And the best part? They absolutely adored it when he curled himself into that perfect, fluffy white ball.

zh:
清明前后总有小雨扰人，街上的行人少了，就连那些总来不羡仙喝酒的常客都没了人影。像这样没生意的日子，寒掌柜倒也没拘着孩子，任由少东家跑出去玩。

少东家在神仙渡见一农户正烧纸祭奠先祖，也觉得有趣。上前看了一会儿还觉不够，找了些废纸也学那人的模样烧了起来。待到日落西山，寒掌柜左等右等也不见少东家回来吃饭，才起身去神仙渡寻人。哪知少东家摇头晃脑的，正在烧纸，口中还念念有词。

那天傍晚，神仙渡不少人都看见了少东家被寒掌柜提回不羡仙。寒掌柜边走还边说：“等我死了你可得给我多烧点，我也想下去过过好日子。”那声音不大不小地回荡在神仙渡。村民们偷笑少东家今晚又要倒霉，转头又开始忙活着回家准备晚饭。

可怜了少东家，到了第二天眼睛还是肿的。只能眯着眼睛，拿着寒掌柜煮的热鸡蛋，继续到处跑。
en:
Qingming Festival always came with a bothersome, gloomy drizzle. Streets became less crowded, and even the regulars of Blissful Retreat gave up their drinks. On such quiet days, Shopkeeper Han allowed the Young Master to go out and play.

At Heaven's Pier, the Young Master noticed a farmer burning joss paper to honor his ancestors. Finding it amusing, the Young Master approached to watch. Then he grabbed some scrap paper and burned it in the same way. Shopkeeper Han waited and waited for the Young Master to come back, but even as the sun began to set, no sign of him appeared. So, she headed towards Heaven's Pier to find the Young Master, and find him, she did—just not in the way she expected. There was a figure swaying from side to side, feeding scraps of joss paper into the fire and mumbling gibberish.

That evening, many people at Heaven's Pier saw the Young Master being brought back to Blissful Retreat by Shopkeeper Han. As they walked, Shopkeeper Han said, "When I die, you'd better burn more joss paper for me. I'd like a life of plenty in the afterlife too." Her stern words carried a warmth that spread throughout Heaven's Pier. The villagers chuckled, sure that the Young Master was going to catch it yet again tonight. Then, they turned back to prepare dinner.

The next day, the poor Young Master still had puffy eyes, barely able to keep them open. Holding a boiled egg Shopkeeper Han had prepared, the Young Master carried on adventuring.

某再拜老师：
自辞山游学，逮乎今日已有月余。吾与师兄一行取道邢州、曲阳，得见石雕、白瓷诸技艺。工法新妙，与山内迥异。后又经高邑、巨鹿、曲周，山州穷绝，渐热难行。更兼州中大旱，乃制水车、连磨诸农器，以纾困局。后闻南面有木构水闸，架设精巧，欲往访之。
途行半道，忽闻恒州兵燹，乱兵肆虐。白骨露野，丘山叠积。鹤长老共封龙书院诸同门，已尽投战事。此中况味，正如病危行汗，存亡须臾，而呼医未至，其荒扰可以想见也。吾与师兄金徵、来沅、付有志、章垚 共议，决意北上援驰。吾等虽无披甲执戈之勇，然怀机巧之术，愿以此术安民守土，兴利除害。
冬月将至，今千万寄此达吾师，望师父善自珍摄，毋为吾念。
en:
I bow respectfully to my Master:
It has been over a month since I left the mountain to travel and study. My senior brothers and I journeyed through Xingzhou and Quyang, where we witnessed the local mastery of stone carving and white porcelain. The techniques were wonderfully novel, vastly different from those within our mountain. Later, we passed through Gaoyi, Julu, and Quzhou; the terrain was rugged and desolate, and the growing heat made our travel difficult. Furthermore, witnessing a severe drought in the region, we constructed waterwheels, linked mills, and other agricultural tools to help ease the people's plight. We then heard of an ingeniously designed wooden watergate to the south and intended to visit it.

Halfway along our journey, we suddenly received word of the fires of war in Hengzhou, where rebel soldiers are running rampant. Exposed bones litter the wilderness, piled as high as hills. Elder Crane and our fellow disciples from Dragonbend Academy have already thrown themselves entirely into the war effort. The situation there is like a critically ill man sweating profusely; life and death are decided in an instant, yet the healer called for has not arrived. The chaos and despair can only be imagined. 

After much deliberation with my senior brothers Jin Zheng, Lai Yuan, Fu Youzhi, and Zhang Yao, we have resolved to head north to offer our aid. Though we lack the courage to don armor and wield halberds, we carry the knowledge of mechanisms. We wish to use these skills to protect the land, comfort the people, promote the good, and eliminate the harmful.

Winter is approaching. I send this letter across a great distance to reach you, my Master, hoping you will take good care of yourself and shed no worry for me.

弟子黄云韶，叩禀师安。
弟子学医，始于师尊笔下丹青。您曾言，医者之针，当如画者之笔，令枯木逢春，为死寂添色。
然今日北境，虏人铁蹄踏碎山河，战火撕裂画卷。王清大侠与众义士死守中渡桥，万千生民罹难，滹沱河畔已成血海。每思及此，弟子心如刀绞，夜不能寐。
弟子深知“一命一价”非为钱货，而是为仁心立威，为医术正名。然弟子常常自问，何以为“价”？沙场之上，救一兵，或可守一寸土；救一将，或可定一战局。我青溪医术，若能为这倾颓之势换取一线生机，这，岂非是比千金更重之“价”？
故，弟子斗胆，欲北上支援。待尘埃落定，云韶甘领责罚。

……
弟子徐芷......
en:
Your disciple Huang Yunshao bows and wishes the Master well.
My medical journey began under your guidance. You once said a physician's needle should be like a painter's brush, bringing spring to withered branches and color to a silent canvas.
But today in the north, the invaders trample our land and tear our world apart. General Wang Qing and the righteous hold fast at Zhongdu Bridge. Hundreds of thousands have perished, and the Hutuo has become a sea of blood. The thought pierces my heart and robs me of sleep.
I understand that "one life, one price" does not speak of trade, but of upholding compassion and the dignity of healing. Yet I often ask myself: what is that "price" truly? On the battlefield, saving a soldier may help hold an inch of ground; saving a general may turn the tide of war. If the medicine of the Silver Needle can win a sliver of hope for this collapsing world, is that not a price weightier than gold?
Therefore, your disciple makes bold to travel north and offer aid. When the dust settles, Yunshao will gladly accept any punishment.

  侠客掌柜大笑，有何不可，三人同饮。
  第二日，侠客不见，唯在天京渡附近余一金叶，契丹满城杀侠客，却遍寻不得，却有风声所言。

en:
In the fourth year of Kaiyun, as the Khitan invaded, a red-sleeved Swordsman entered the city upon hearing a tavern owner planned to host the enemy. But instead of a traitor, the hero found an ally—the shopkeeper had set a trap to burn the building and slay the Khitan.
The two fought side by side, wiped out the enemy, and shared a final jar of wine atop the bones of their foes, fire blazing, wine fragrant.
A beggar named Zheng appeared, seeking food for a dying brother. Moved by his loyalty, they invited him to join. He had nothing but a grass-woven leaf.
They laughed—"Why not?"—and drank as one.
The next day, the hero vanished, leaving only a golden leaf by the Tianjing Dock. The Khitan searched the city in vain. All that remained were whispers...
That night, a nameless figure stepped into #YHopewell Academy#E.

【周书·泰誓中】

惟戊午，王次于河朔，群后以师毕会。
王乃徇师而誓曰：“呜呼！西土有众，咸听朕言。我闻吉人为善，惟日不足；凶人为不善，亦惟日不足。今商王受，力行无度，播弃犁老，昵比罪人。淫酗肆虐，臣下化之，朋家作仇，胁权相灭，无辜吁天，秽德彰闻。
“惟天惠民，惟辟奉天。有夏桀弗克若天，流毒下国。天乃佑命成汤，降黜夏命，惟受罪浮于桀，剥丧元良，贼虐谏辅。谓已有天命，谓敬不足行，谓祭无益，谓暴无伤。厥监惟不远，在彼夏王。天其以予乂民。朕梦协朕卜，袭于休祥，戎商必克；受有亿兆夷人，离心离德。予有乱臣十人，同心同德。虽有周亲，不如仁人。
“天视自我民视，天听自我民听。百姓有过，在予一人，今朕必往。
“我武惟扬，侵于之疆，取彼凶残。我伐用张，于汤有光。
“勖哉夫子，罔或无畏，宁执非敌。百姓懔懔，若崩厥角。呜呼！乃一德一心，立定厥功，惟克永世。”
en:
【Book of Zhou · Great Declaration II】

On the day Wu Wu, the king halted at the northern bank of the Yellow River, and all the feudal lords gathered with their troops in full assembly.
The king then reviewed the army and made an oath, saying: "Alas! All you multitudes of the western lands, listen carefully to my words. I have heard that when good men do good deeds, they find even a full day insufficient; when wicked men do evil, they too find even a full day insufficient. Now King Shou of Shang, exerting himself in lawlessness, has cast aside the aged and wise, and drawn close to sinners. Drunken and wanton, tyrannical and cruel, his ministers and officers have imitated him, forming factions and making enemies of one another, wielding power to destroy each other. The innocent cry out to Heaven, and his foul virtue is manifest to all.
"Heaven loves the people, and the sovereign should honor Heaven. Jie of Xia failed to comply with Heaven, spreading calamity throughout the realm. Heaven then favored and commanded Tang the Completer, deposing the mandate of Xia. Now Shou's crimes exceed those of Jie: he has destroyed the good and virtuous, and cruelly persecuted his remonstrating ministers. He claims he possesses Heaven's mandate, deems reverence unnecessary, considers sacrifice worthless, and regards violence as harmless. His mirror is not far off—it is that Xia king. Heaven will use me to govern the people. My dreams accord with my divinations, both auspicious omens; we shall surely conquer Shang. Shou has hundreds of millions of common people, yet they are divided in heart and virtue. I have ten capable ministers, united in heart and virtue. Though he has many close relatives, they are not as good as my virtuous men.
"Heaven sees as my people see; Heaven hears as my people hear. If the common people have faults, they rest on me alone. Now I must go forth.
"Let my martial might be displayed, invading their territory, seizing that cruel and vicious one. My campaign shall be magnified, bringing glory even to Tang.
"Strive on, my officers! Do not be reckless or fearless, but rather hold firm as if facing an enemy. The people tremble in fear, as if their horns were broken in submission. Alas! Be of one virtue and one heart, establish your achievements firmly, and you shall endure for all generations."

zh:
河伯的威名，开封无人不晓。只是河伯究竟何许人也，城中人却莫衷一是。
有人说，河伯多是博浪张氏，也曾有掌河洛漕运的威名，自汉武时便雄踞一方，却一时不慎，身子一软，做了契丹人的狗，也便再不好论及此人了。
有人说，河伯多是龙蛟帮中人，青衣红袖，傩面覆面，扇剑同修，悬壶济世，便是当年契丹一战中，功名赫赫的朱鱼帮主。
还有人说，这河伯……不过是一个名姓，应一声，便要遭一辈子大罪，此生汲汲，再无他路。众人瞧定，何人竟敢口出狂言，却只见不过一区区咸鱼郎，叼了根狗尾巴草，趿拉着草鞋，睡眼惺忪。“市井笑话，随口胡言，不然……客官瞧瞧这咸鱼，都是尖儿货。”众人哄笑而散，毕竟咸鱼货郎的话，自古又有谁人当真？

冯夷不喜欢被拘在一处，江湖这般大，本便该四海遨游，任侠天地。可冯夷又不得不被拘在一处，因为开封百姓都被拘到了一处——契丹人刀下。开封城破之时，普通人不成为两脚羊，便已算是最好的结局了，救死扶伤的总是江湖豪侠，又关小小咸鱼郎何事？冯夷本可如此自嘲，谁料走在已空无一人的封丘村，却有契丹猛将横空劈下一刀。

英雄救美的故事，话本里写得多。可冯夷膀大腰圆，不是什么美人，更不是什么英雄。眼前绿衣红袖的女子，一横剑击退了契丹人，转身一脚，又将冯夷踩在了脚下。这下咸鱼总算翻不了身——被一脚钉在了地上。这样的开场实在不能算作浪漫，虽然那救命的一剑已足够扣人心弦。

很久之后冯夷才知道，那时的朱鱼同燃灯僧一起熬制茱萸汤，早已精疲力竭，就像很久之后，冯夷才愿意喝下朱萸汤，选择加入龙蛟帮一样。朱鱼麾下的龙蛟帮众，也都是普通人：长着普通样貌、使着普通武艺、过着普通生死，却有着与普通毫无关系的豪情壮志：今时今刻，驱逐契丹，来年来日，黄河波平，不兴风雨。这些话，常人说的不信，可不知为何，从她嘴里说出，便有了万钧之力，无人不信。

“今时今刻，驱逐契丹，来年来日，黄河波平，不兴风雨。”连咸鱼郎也不禁如此喃喃起来。
en:
The River Master's name carried weight in Kaifeng. But who the River Master truly was remained a mystery.

Some said the River Master was a member of the Zhang clan of Roaring Sands, once influential in the river transport trade since the Han Dynasty, only to fall from grace and serve the Khitan as dogs.
Others said the River Master was part of the Dragon Hall, wearing blue robes, red sleeves, and Nuo Dance Mask, skilled with both sword and fan, and known for healing the sick. This was the same Zhu Yu who had earned her fame in the Khitan wars.

Still, others whispered that the River Master was just a name, a cursed title that brought endless suffering. Those who carried it lived a life of toil, with no other path to follow. When people turned to see who dared speak such blasphemy, they found only a salty fish vendor, chewing on a blade of grass, wearing straw sandals, and looking half-asleep. "Just a market joke, nothing serious. Or hey, take a look at this salted fish, top quality!" The crowd burst into laughter, dismissing the vendor's words. After all, who would take a fishmonger seriously?

Feng Yi, for one, hated being confined. The jianghu was vast, meant to be roamed freely. Yet he couldn't escape his confinement, just as Kaifeng's people had been trapped under the blades of the Khitan. When the city fell, ordinary people were lucky if they weren't slaughtered like livestock. Heroes and outlaws stepped up to save lives, but what did that have to do with a mere fishmonger like Feng Yi? He could have laughed at himself for the thought, but as he wandered through the abandoned Verdant Hill Village, a Khitan warrior suddenly brought a blade crashing down on him.

Stories of heroes saving damsels in distress were common in the storybooks. But Feng Yi wasn't a damsel, nor a hero. The green-robed, red-sleeved woman before him deflected the Khitan's blade with a single stroke, then turned and stomped him into the ground. That was how the salted fish vendor met his match, pinned underfoot. It wasn't exactly romantic, though the sword that saved his life was unforgettable.

It was not until much later that Feng Yi learned that Zhu Yu had been exhausted that day, brewing medicinal soup with the Lamp-lighting Monk. And much later still, he would drink Zhu Yu's soup and join the Dragon Hall. The gang members under Zhu Yu were ordinary people: plain in appearance, average in skill, living lives as fragile as anyone else's. Yet their courage and ambition were anything but ordinary. Today, we drive out the Khitans. Tomorrow, we'll calm the Yellow River, bringing peace and ending the storms. Ordinary people wouldn't believe such words. 这禁中诸库怕是皇城里人气最稀薄的地界，阴森森的，米面粮油堆得比山高，看着比活人多。
不过此处守备松懈，正好让我喘口气。只是这院子静得有些渗人，站久了直打哆嗦，也不知看守是如何熬过这漫漫长夜的。
再往里探，是军器库。远远看着那些长枪重甲，便觉一股肃杀之气扑面而来。
不过，那肃杀之气里倒是夹着一股——酒香！醇厚醉人，定是御赐佳酿！不写了不写了，既然来了，若不顺手尝上一口，岂不辜负？先去也！
en:
These treasuries in the palace are probably the most deserted corner of the Imperial City. The whole place feels bleak, with mountains of food and supplies, almost outnumbering the living.

Still, the guard here is lax, which suits me just fine and gives me a chance to catch my breath. But the courtyard is so quiet it gets under your skin. If I stay still for too long, I'd be shivering away. I don't know how the watchmen endure the endless nights.

Farther in lies the armory. Even from a distance, those long spears and heavy suits of armor seem to give off a murderous aura.

And yet, mixed in with it all is something else, the smell of wine. Rich and heady, it's surely a fine royal vintage. Enough writing. Since I'm here, it would be a shame not to sneak a taste. Off I go!
HyperrAven

zh:
游侠在山崖之下收拾着行囊。等收拾完了，他的朋友也该掉下来了。
念头刚落，弄潮儿便从山崖上滑下，精准地朝着游侠的小腿铲去。游侠的头撞到了身后刚收拾好的行囊，弄潮儿的腿趁乱朝着游侠的腰窝踹了一脚，两人这才避免一同落入灼烧的篝火。
游侠被踢懵了。他扶着腰坐起来，怔愣地望着对面哈哈大笑的弄潮儿。

怎地你掉下来没事儿，反倒给我踹得七零八落的！
无心之举，不是故意。
拿两把破刀非要爬最后一遭，还让我在底下等着，就是拉我给你垫背。
那你也垫了。刀破了，我不爬了。
你不过关了？

弄潮儿将两把刀往脚下一插。
凉州何其大，河西何其辽。我一个人过关，又有何用。穷我一生，一定能找到带所有人过关的方法。这刀，便替我在此日日望着大散关吧。
弄潮儿起身，大步往凉州的方向走去。游侠匆匆收好行囊追上他。

让所有人都过关么？
游侠望着怀中之物，又看了看前方意气风发的友人。
或许，此物可以托付给他……
en:
A wanderer packs his bag beneath the cliff, waiting for his friend to fall. 
Just then, Young Yichao slides down, aiming straight for the wanderer's legs. The wanderer's head hits the packed bag; Chao kicks his waist—both narrowly avoid tumbling into the fire. 
Dazed, the wanderer sits up, clutching his side, staring at the laughing Nongchao'er. 

How come you're fine, but I'm the one falling apart? 
Not on purpose. 
You insisted on climbing with two broken blades, made me wait below—just to cushion your fall. 
Well, you did cushion it. Blades are broken, I'm done climbing. 
You're not passing through? 

Young Yichao plants the blades into the ground. 
Liangzhou is vast, the Hexi boundless. What use is passing through alone? In my lifetime, I'll find a way to bring everyone through. Let these blades watch Dasan Pass every day. 
He strides back toward Liangzhou. The wanderer hurriedly packs and follows. 

Bring everyone through? 
The wanderer glances at what he holds, then at his spirited friend ahead. 
Perhaps... this can be entrusted to him...
Heh... so greedy...

Rice gleams with oil, millet glows white. Both public and private granaries are full.
Outside Kaifeng City lies a vast plain of fertile fields, feeding the countless mouths of the realm.
At its heart sits Ever-Normal Granary, a lifeline of the people, built for the public good.
The granary's purpose is to keep grain prices stable, whether harvests are good or bad. By smoothing out the extremes of feast and famine, the granary earns its name: Ever-Normal.
Yet good harvests are hard to come by, and peaceful days harder still. Outside the granary, on the great Plainfield, one side rejoices, the other weeps. One grain of wheat, one kernel of millet, each weighs with it the fate of the people.

He also created mountain scenes where the figures juggled balls, threw swords, climbed ropes, and stood upside down, moving in and out freely. He went on to build miniature offices of officials, with figures grinding grain and making fighting cocks, showcasing countless ingenious variations.

zh:
太平钟楼下，敲钟老人的箫声依旧。你的到来并未打断他的闲情。箫声一转，如泣如诉。你不是第一次来到这里，但这一次，你似乎听出了曲中的故事。那是汤汤洛水与皓皓白雪的交锋，是凛冽寒梅与清澈深泉的对望，是一对恋人变作怨侣的转折，是情与义落下至真至痛的一笔，是从此天涯陌路人的诀别。你知道故事里的人是谁，可那场大战她从没对你提起，你也不知最后是谁赢了。老人似乎看出你所想，将同样的问题抛给了你。你思索片刻，回答道……
#Y两败俱伤。你在弱水岸见过无面人的残驱，也听闻过悬剑北上的壮举。也许他和她都没赢——他们失去了彼此的心，也阔别了彼此的命。#E
老人微笑，不置可否。他向你缓缓讲述着故事的余料。悬剑之义，天泉之义，洛神之义，燕北盟之义……每个人都站在了道义的箭锋之上，而引弦之手，从不由人。
en:
Beneath the Peace Bell Tower, the old bell-ringer's flute still sings as ever. Your arrival does nothing to disturb his quiet ease. Then the melody shifted, weeping and whispering like a grief too deep for words. This is not your first time here, yet this time, you seem at last to hear the story hidden within the song.
It is the clash between the surging Luo River and the gleaming white snow; the silent gaze between bitter winter plum and a deep, clear spring. It is the turning point where lovers become estranged, the stroke where love and duty leave their truest, most agonizing mark, the final parting that leaves them as strangers at the ends of the earth. You know who the story is about. Yet she has never spoken of that great battle, and you never learned who emerged victorious in the end. The old man seems to read your thoughts, tossing the same question back to you. After a moment's reflection, you give your answer...
#YMutual ruin. On the Still Shore, you've seen the mangled remains of the Faceless One, and heard tales of Hanging Blade's heroic journey north. Perhaps neither emerged victorious. They lost each other's hearts, and forever parted from each other's fates.#E
The old man only smiles, neither confirming nor denying it. Slowly, he recounts the untold fragments of the tale: the honor of the Hanging Blade, the honor of Well of Heaven, the honor of Water Lady, the honor of the Northern Vow… Each stood balanced upon the arrowhead of honor, yet the hand that drew the bowstring was never their own.

zh:
涌泉镇的人都知道，胡老头只在蒙学馆前卖糖饼，得闲的时候，他就站在门口，看着孩子们摇头晃脑地跟着先生念书。
真是赶上好日子了，正堂那时候哪有这家门口的学堂，胡老头心想。
那时候，涌泉镇还没有蒙学馆，胡老头走街串巷卖煎饼，每挣几个铜板，就塞进床底下的瓦罐里。正堂要念书，先生家却是隔着三十里地。天不亮就得动身，翻一座山，蹚一条河，才能在午课前赶到。
每次出门，胡老头都把粗粮煎饼叠得整整齐齐，用油纸包了，塞进正堂的布褡裢。临了，他从灶台最里层摸出一枚糖饼——红糖化开，麻酱抹匀，面饼烙得两面金黄——小心翼翼地放进褡裢最深处。
糖贵了，他只舍得放一枚，正堂走路累了、读书饿了，能有个甜头。
后来正堂争气，一路从童生考到举人。再后来，那封家书寄到了。
胡老头把那封信翻来覆去读了不知多少遍，每一个字都像烙在心口上。他杀了家里仅有的那只鸡，去镇上打了酒，把糖饼烙了满满一锅，见人就发——“中咧，俺家正堂中咧！”
他没有等到正堂。
消息是县衙的差役带回来的，早悟寺那带的水泊闹匪，返乡的举子们遭了劫。
胡老头听完，站了很久。然后转身进屋，把那一锅已经凉透的糖饼一块一块吃完，嚼得很慢，一点声音都没有。
第二天清晨，他推着独轮车，出现在蒙学馆门口。
从那以后，涌泉镇的孩子们多了一个念想——胡老头的糖饼，又大又甜，芝麻撒得满满当当，红糖和麻酱抹了厚厚一层，咬一口能甜到嗓子眼。
en:
Everyone in Wellspring Town knows that Elder Hu sells his sweet pancakes exclusively outside the Primary Hall. Whenever he has a spare moment, he stands by the doorway, watching the children sway in rhythm as they recite their lessons after the master.
Such blessed times these children live in, Elder Hu often thinks to himself. Back in Zheng Tang's day, there was no primary school right on the doorstep.
Back then, Wellspring Town didn't have an academy. Elder Hu used to walk the streets and alleys peddling savory flatbreads, dropping whatever meager coppers he earned into a clay pot hidden beneath his bed. Zheng Tang was determined to learn, but the nearest tutor lived ten miles away. The boy had to set out long before dawn, crossing a mountain and wading across a river, just to make it in time for afternoon lessons.
Before every journey, Elder Hu would neatly stack coarse-grain flatbreads, wrap them in oiled paper, and tuck them into Zheng Tang's cloth satchel. Then, at the very last moment, he would reach to the back of the stove and pull out a single sweet pancake, its brown sugar perfectly melted, the sesame paste spread thick, the dough toasted to a golden crisp. Carefully, he would slip it into the very bottom of the boy's bag.
Sugar was a luxury, so he could only afford to include one. It was a small comfort, just enough to give Zheng Tang a taste of sweetness when the miles left him exhausted or his studies left him hungry.
Zheng Tang did him proud, rising through the ranks to pass the provincial exams. And then came the day when that letter arrived.
Elder Hu read the letter over and over again, every single character etching itself into his heart. He slaughtered his only chicken, bought wine in town, and griddled a massive, overflowing batch of sweet pancakes. He handed them out to everyone he crossed paths with, beaming and shouting, "He passed! My Zheng Tang passed!"
But Zheng Tang never came home.
The news was brought by runners from the county court. Bandits had ambushed the marshlands near Seedling Temple, and the scholars journeying home had been caught in the slaughter.
Hearing the news, Elder Hu stood frozen for a long, long time. Finally, he turned around, walked into his empty house, and ate the entire batch of stone-cold sugar pancakes. He ate them one by one, chewing slowly, in absolute, unbroken silence.
The very next morning, he pushed his wheelbarrow out and set up at the gates of the Primary Hall.

Ever since that day, the children of Wellspring Town have had a special treat to look forward to. Elder Hu's sugar pancakes are impossibly large and sweet, generously showered in sesame seeds, and slathered with such a thick layer of brown sugar and sesame paste that a single bite leaves a lingering sweetness all the way down to the soul.

zh:
变故发生在广政十七年。王团花好不容易见到前唐名家张素卿所画的十二幅《十二仙真像》，一时手痒，便将十二幅图描了个遍。可画却不翼而飞。直到一件事震惊蜀国上下。

这年蜀王大寿，大臣安思谦将《十二仙真像》呈送蜀王。可没多久，蜀王接到秘报，称此画乃是伪作。蜀王本就想除去安思谦，便借此机会将其杀了，誓要将余党一网打尽。而那画，正是王团花画的。此后蜀中画坛便有传言，说那画乃是一弱冠少年伪作，人们称其为“十二仙”。

没有人在意他的画有多出色，王团花——现在应该叫他“十二仙”了——莫名成了被追查的“余党”。王家上下为此操碎了心，想尽办法将他送出蜀国，让他在中原避些时日。终于，再也没有人叫他“王团花”了，再也没有一个家可以让他逃了。

他开始觉得，也许自己那所谓的天赋有另一个名字——诅咒。可他又觉得自己很委屈，明明他什么都没做，为什么要离开？为什么要怕？到了中原，他开始对外声称，自己就是“十二仙”。此时的他尚且年轻，不知道蜀王需要的只是把戏做足，而他不过是其中一枚小小的棋子。他当然不知道，《十二仙真像》是谁让他见到的。

十二仙消沉了好些日子，他的画不再有生机，像是被抽干了灵魂。
en:
The turning point came in the 17th year of the Guangzheng era. Wang Tuanhua finally laid eyes on the twelve Portraits of Twelve Immortals by Zhang Suqing, a renowned Tang painter. Unable to resist, he copied all twelve pieces. But the copies vanished without a trace until a scandal shook the Shu Kingdom.

That year, on the Shu King's birthday, Minister An Siqian presented the Twelve Immortals as a gift. Soon after, the King received a tip that the paintings were forgeries. Already plotting An's downfall, the King seized the opportunity to execute him, vowing to eliminate all "conspirators". And those forgeries? They were Wang Tuanhua's work. Overnight, rumors spread in Shu's art circles: a young man in his twenties had forged the paintings, and he became known as "the Twelve Immortals".

No one cared about his talent. Wang Tuanhua—now "Twelve Immortals"—was suddenly a hunted "conspirator." His family risked everything to smuggle him out of Shu, sending him to hide in the Central Plains. At last, no one called him "Wang Tuanhua" any more, but neither did he have a home to flee to.He began to see his gift as a curse. Why should he suffer? He'd done nothing wrong. In the Central Plains, he embraced the name "Twelve Immortals", too young to realize the Shu King's purge was a charade, and he merely a pawn. Of course, he didn't know who had arranged for him to "discover" Zhang Suqing's originals in the first place.

For months, Twelve Immortals spiraled. His paintings lost their vitality, as if their soul had been drained.

en:
The Reach
Female, appearance unknown. Skilled in Lightness, she often slips into wealthy homes under cover of night. Eccentric by nature, she delights in hanging her victims' private letters and account books from city tower flagpoles and other lofty places, all to stir up a spectacle. This thief is extremely swift. If spotted, do not pursue on your own. Report her to the authorities at once.
Silken Fox
Highly skilled in disguise, with a glib tongue to match. She often poses as someone close to the household to slip inside. According to reports, her appearance changes constantly. At times she seems a frail old woman, at times a delicate scholar. Cunning to the extreme. All gatekeepers are hereby warned to inspect visitors carefully and not be deceived by appearances.
Kongkong
Male, appearance unknown. A notorious thief in Kaifeng, he knows its streets, drains, and rooftops inside out, and has escaped more than once by using the terrain. His movements are unpredictable. If he is sighted, do not alert him. Report it to the authorities immediately so they can move in and cut off his escape.
Ground Ghost
Appearance unknown. Some witnesses claim the figure resembles a child. This thief specializes in tunneling underground. At each crime scene, sudden cave-ins are often found, and investigation reveals tunnels leading straight into storehouses. The traces left behind could not have been made by human strength alone, suggesting the use of some ingenious device. Citizens are hereby warned: if you hear strange sounds beneath the ground at night, stay alert.

zh: 噫，余访山历水多矣，何尝见梦中世界乎？今日访之，竟比仙境。千树梨花盛开，落英缤纷，入水随波而去，水畔酒客流觞，奏琴伴饮，酒香弥野。入暮有打铁花之艺，滚沸铁水抛洒于空，似星落如雨。观者如云，甚是热闹。余观此间山水地貌、人情风俗，几与不羡仙相同，然略有区别。余曾恨不羡仙毁于兵燹，再无离人泪可享，今日得见梦中世界，不由兴起一吟谪仙之句：桃花流水杳然去，别有天地非人间。

Thousands of pear trees bloom in full splendor, their petals falling in a riot of color, drifting into the water and flowing away with the current. By the riverside, drunk scholars float wine goblets on the stream, playing guqins as they drink—the aroma of wine fills the wilderness. At dusk, artisans perform the iron flower fireworks: boiling molten iron is tossed into the air, scattering like stars raining down. Crowds of onlookers gather, creating a lively scene. The landscape and customs here almost mirror those of Blissful Retreat, yet with subtle differences. I once lamented that Blissful Retreat was destroyed in war, no longer offering Parting Tears to savor. But today, seeing this dreamworld, I can't help but recite a line from the Banished Immortal (Li Bai): "Peach blossoms and flowing water vanish far away; this is a realm apart, not of the mortal world."

The stray was thin and small, crouching on Luna's favorite rock, quietly watching the night sky.
Luna offered her warm tail... and from then on, this rock became their shared secret base.

第一式，市井藏身术：
别管是土路还是水路，要行万里路，总得挑只好船，渡口虽大，也需混入码头，方可一览众船。诸君且想，倘若不曾好好挑船，船板不牢，船至半路，沉底了，那岂不是白费功夫，还得搭上一条小命？
混迹码头，自然是猫有猫道，鼠有鼠道——无论是摆摊，打小工，还是上船卸货，都各有优劣。据闲人调查，摆摊虽然自由，但据船太远，只可远观，并无机会上船；码头处店家众多，打小工自然消息灵通，足可掌握第一流行船消息，可惜东家不许多嘴多打听，有时还需盘账，搬货，背书，实在是辛苦——唯有卸货，既可上船，又可下船，甚至能亲测船板是否牢靠，就是太花力气！
果然啊，世上并无十全十美之事！
……
第二式，半夜摸船法：
想必看到此处的各位早已完成了第一步，挑着了心仪好船，倘若未曾挑中，请耐心翻至第一招，静静等待缘分中的那艘船。
如今，你已经看中了一艘船，而它必然会在渡口过上不止一夜，而半夜！博易务是不接待船只的！我等起码有一夜时间！
请诸君着重读以下内容，必要时可以背诵，确保一字不差，若稍有差池，只怕谋算彻底落空！牢记！
（三页被撕走了）

第三式，忍饿保命功：
所谓天将降大任于斯人也，必先苦其心志，劳其筋骨，看官暂且忍饥挨饿一段时间，实在饿得受不了，尽可打劫船上的粮仓，倘若被发现，也可自告奋勇做船上劳工，多干一份力气活，自然能拿一份吃食——等水至尽头，航船靠岸，瞒天过海也就成了，诸位自可周游天下，一览风景！
切记切记，莫把我这闲人供出来！
……
en:
Still stressing over travel money? Dreaming of adventuring across the jianghu, but completely broke? Well, I've got too much time on my hands today, so I'm sharing some free advice to point my fellow broke wanderers in the right direction!
...
Step 1: Blending in at the Ferries
To go the distance, you're going to need a good ship. But to take your pick of the fleet, you first have to find a way to fit in at the ferries. Think about it: if you don't pick a sturdy boat and it sinks halfway to your destination, you haven't just wasted your time. You've lost your life!
Surviving the ferries means playing the game, and you've got three main options: running a street stall, working odd jobs, or unloading cargo. They all have their pros and cons. Running a stall gives you freedom, but it keeps you too far from the water to actually board anything. Working at the ferry shops keeps you in the loop on all the shipping schedules, but owners hate a nosy worker, and the constant tallying, hauling, and memorizing can be a headache. Unloading cargo is the only gig that lets you move freely between the ferry and the boats. You even get to test how sturdy the deck is for yourself! The downside? It's backbreaking work.
Hey, nothing in this world is perfect!
...
Step 2: The Midnight Boarding
If you're reading this, you've presumably finished step one and spotted the ship of your dreams. If not, go back to step one and wait patiently for the right vessel to come along.
Now, any ship you choose is bound to dock for at least one night. And at midnight, the Maritime Trade Bureau shuts down! That gives us a window to make our move!
Read this next part extremely carefully. Memorize it word for word if you have to. A single mistake, and the whole plan goes up in smoke!
(Three pages have been torn out)

Step 3: Starving and Surviving
You know what they say: before greatness is achieved, you must first suffer through hardship. Just grit your teeth and deal with the hunger for a while. If you truly can't take it anymore, you can try sneaking into the ship's pantry. If you get caught, just volunteer to join the crew. Do some heavy lifting, and they'll feed you. Once the ship reaches its final destination, you're in the clear, and the world is yours to explore!
Just remember one thing: whatever happens, do not rat me out!
...

Oh, it's just you.

zh:
村里人都说，帆子迟早要走。
这话从他进村头一天就有人说。文津馆出来的读书人，考了吏员分下来，不过是镀层金，待个一年半载就调走了。
帆子也不辩解。他嘴笨，越想说清楚越说不清楚。
他跑镇上种子铺，站了一个月，把新麦种磨回来了。那年秋里收成多了两成。孙大爷蹲在地头看着沉甸甸的麦穗，半天没说话，站起来拍了拍他肩膀，走了。
村里修路，有人不愿出工。他扛着铁锹替人家干了三天。第四天那人自己来了，啥也没说，低头干活。
他娘来给他送腌咸菜，看见他眼睛底下那两坨青、床头堆满的手记、磨穿了底的布鞋，说要不回家吧。
他摇头。“娘，这村里一百多户人，我能叫出每一户的名。谁家老人要吃药，谁家地该浇水，我都知道。我走了，这些事就没人管了。”
后来县里来了文书，调他回县衙当书吏。他把文书压在《农政全书》底下，三天没睡好。第四天去找村长，把文书放桌上。
“村长，我不走。”
“想好了？”
“想好了。”
到如今，还是有人问，帆子你真不走啊。他就笑，不说话。
孙大爷替他说了：“他走啥。他比咱村的人还像咱村的人。”
窗外葱田青青的，望不到头。
en:
The village had him figured out from day one: Fan wouldn't be sticking around.
Everyone knew how the system worked. Young scholars out of the Inkbound Order only took these rural magistrate postings as a stepping stone. Give it six months to a year, and he'd be off to a comfortable promotion in the city.
Yang Fan never tried to argue. He wasn't much of a talker anyway.
The harder he tried to explain himself, the more tongue-tied he got.
He spent a solid month wearing down the seed merchant in town until he finally scored a new, hardier strain of wheat for the village. That autumn, the harvest jumped by twenty percent. Old Man Sun just squatted by the fields, staring at the heavy, golden stalks in total silence. After a long while, the old man stood up, clapped Yang Fan on the shoulder, and walked away.
Later, when it was time to repair the local roads, a few folks refused to pitch in. Yang Fan didn't complain. He just picked up a shovel and did their share of the backbreaking work for three days straight. On the fourth day, one of the holdouts showed up without a word, grabbed a shovel of his own, and got to work.
When his mother came to drop off a fresh jar of pickled vegetables, she took one look at the dark bags under his eyes, the mountain of worn notebooks by his bed, and the holes eaten clean through the soles of his shoes. Softly, she told him it was time to come home.
Yang Fan shook his head. "Mum, there are over a hundred families in this village, and I know every single one by name. I know whose elders need their medicine, and whose fields need watering. If I leave, who's going to look out for them?"
Eventually, the inevitable happened. An official transfer order arrived, offering him a prestigious desk job back at the County Court. Yang Fan shoved the letter under a heavy book titled Agricultural Administration and didn't sleep a wink for three nights. On the fourth day, he walked into the village chief's house and dropped the letter on the table.
"Chief, I'm not leaving."
"You sure about that?"
"I'm sure."
Even now, folks will stop him on the road and ask, "Fan, are you really staying?" Yang Fan just smiles.
These days, Old Man Sun is the one who answers for him. "Where's he going?" the old man huffs, taking a slow drag from his pipe. "Boy belongs to this village more than the rest of us do."
Outside the window, the vibrant green of the leek fields stretches on, as far as the eye can see.
Zhou the Lame

zh:
一更了。今夜敲梆子的是老孙头，我听得出来。
他的梆子声比旁人轻，轻里带着颤——从前不是这样的。从前他总把梆子敲得又重又脆，但那天之后，他便再也敲不出那样的声了。
梆子一下，两下……孙老头走得很慢，但还是越走越远了。也只有他，从不往这殿的窗格里瞧。他的眼睛空茫茫的，像蒙着秋雾的井。
我也是。
我们都在那场雨里湿透过。

那是乾佑元年的秋。那天的雨，真大啊，砸在殿瓦上，像是老天爷也在捶鼓鸣冤。
可殿内静得骇人。
乌泱泱的官老爷们立在那里，像一片黑压压的树林。他们的眼长在头顶，心藏在脚下。
他们都知道李大人为何而死。
他因忠直而死，因知恩而死，因党祸而死。
但圣意已然劈下，那么他的死就得换个缘由。
——“谋危社稷，潜结奸凶，拟为叛乱。”
这字字句句，将他砸进了烂泥里。谁也没再说什么，谁也说不得什么。
风雨要竹子弯，它便只能折。满殿的人看着它折，看着它碎，看着它被泥水卷走。然后他们沉默转身，各自撑开了伞。
我也有一把伞。我死死攥着它，指甲嵌进伞柄里。可我最终，没有往前迈那一步。
于是李大人的叹息，就那么融进了这皇宫的上空。与每次大典乐声的消散那般，无甚差别。

漫天的雨水落下来，一滴，又一滴，敲在砖上，声音比此刻老孙头的梆子还清楚。
我没有错。一个小内侍，连头顶的半寸天都撑不起，更何论去辩一场已定的局？
两年了，我每晚都这么对自己嘀咕，像念一道保命的符。可这道符镇不住梦——梦里下着好大的雨，从不停歇。
上个月，和老孙头吃酒。酒冷了，他忽然没头没尾地说：“李大人……从前最爱笑我的梆子声。” 说完他就笑了，笑得比哭还难听。
从前他总说，人活一世，要对得起祖宗牌位。如今他只说，酒冷了，得热一热。
我们都学会了喝冷酒，说热话。

那一滴，一滴的雨，就这样渗了好些年。从殿外的砖缝，渗到了这殿的地上，渗进了我的骨头里。而我还在写。
这些字，会被虫蛀，被灰埋，或许永远等不到被看见的一天。
那我写什么呢？写给自己听吗？写给后人看吗？
我不知道。
我只觉得冷，月色照亮了我脚下的砖地，却照不到我。
在这个夜晚，在过去的很多个夜晚，在之后的更多个夜晚……都照不到我。
en:
The first watch. Old Sun is striking the clapper tonight. I can tell. His clapper is softer than the others, soft with a tremor. It was not always so. He used to strike it heavy and crisp, but after that day he never could again.

One knock, then another. Old Sun walks slowly, yet the sound still drifts farther and farther away. Only he never glances at the lattice windows of this hall. His eyes are blank, like a well filmed over with autumn mist. Mine are the same. We were both soaked through in that rain.

It was the autumn of Qianyou Year 1. The rain was brutal, pounding the palace tiles as if Heaven itself were beating a drum to cry injustice. Inside the hall, the silence was worse. The officials stood packed together like a dark forest. Their eyes were set high; their hearts were buried low.

They all knew why Lord Li died. He died for being loyal and straight. He died for repaying a debt. He died for the calamity of factional strife. But once the imperial verdict came down, his death needed a different cause.

"He conspired against the state, secretly allied with traitors and villains, and plotted rebellion."

Each word drove him into the mud. No one said a thing. No one could. When wind and rain demand that bamboo bend, it can only bend until it breaks. Everyone in the hall watched it bend, watched it snap, watched it swept away in the mire. Then they turned in silence and opened their umbrellas.

I had one too. I gripped the handle so hard my nails bit in. In the end, I did not take that step forward.

So Lord Li's sigh seeped into the air above this palace, no different from how the music of every grand ceremony rises and fades.

The rain kept falling, drop after drop, striking the bricks more clearly than Old Sun's clapper does now. I was not wrong. I was a lowly palace attendant. I could not even hold up the half inch of sky above my own head, let alone argue a case already decided.

For two years I have muttered this to myself every night, like a charm to stay alive. It cannot hold back the dream. In the dream, the rain is heavy and never stops.

Last month I drank with Old Sun. The wine had gone cold when he said, out of nowhere, "Lord Li... used to laugh at my clapper the most." Then he laughed, and it sounded worse than crying.

He used to say a man should live so he would not shame his ancestors' tablets. Now he only says the wine is cold and needs warming. We have both learned to drink cold wine and speak warm words.

Drop by drop, that rain has seeped on for years, from the cracks in the bricks outside, onto this hall's floor, and into my bones. And still I write. These words will be eaten by insects, buried in dust, perhaps never seen.

So why do I write? For myself? For those who come after?

I do not know. I only know I am cold. The moonlight spills over the bricks at my feet, but it cannot reach me. Not tonight. Not on the many nights before. Not on the many nights to come.

作为骆驼夫，佰滥时常都在摸鱼。他是一个很不让人放心的人，认识他的朋友、长辈都不敢将自己的事儿交给他来做，但这样也正好遂了他的愿。
他对一切紧急的、危险的、迫切的事情都淡淡的。当别人急得如热锅上的蚂蚁时，他的一句“那又咋了”更火上浇油。“那又咋了”是他的口头禅，也是他面对一切事情的应对之法。他极力避免任何让他感到不适或压力的事情，宁愿停留在舒适区里，他认为一切挑战和困难都是没事找事，还不如让自己身心舒适，凡事都比不上让自己身体健康、心情放松。交给他办的事，他永远都会糊弄过去，非必要不干活，骆驼活着就行。有的时候，他也会糊弄得过于明显，比如经常说：”啊，怎么会这样？“、”真的吗？“、”不是吧！！“、”这个也太那个吧！!“、"哦，太难了，太难了，换我受不了这个"来糊弄别人。
en:
As a camel driver, Bai Lan often slacks off. He is a very unreliable person, friends and elders who know him dare not entrust him with anything, but this is exactly what he wants. 
He is indifferent to all urgent, dangerous, or pressing matters. When others are anxious like ants on a hot pan, his catchphrase "So what?" only adds fuel to the fire. "So what?" is not only his mantra but also his way of dealing with everything. He tries his best to avoid anything that makes him uncomfortable or stressed, preferring to stay in his comfort zone. He believes that all challenges and difficulties are unnecessary troubles, it's better to keep himself physically and mentally comfortable, nothing is more important than his health and relaxation. He always muddles through tasks assigned to him, refusing to work unless absolutely necessary, as long as the camels are alive. Sometimes his pretense is too obvious, and he often uses phrases like "Ah, how could this happen?", "Really?", "No way!!", "This is too much!", or "Oh, it's so hard, so hard. I can't stand this" to fool others.

In the Tang era, the Wanghu Pavilion was built here, where one gazed upon a boundless lake glowing in autumn's single hue—hence its name, Autumn Moon on the Calm Lake. It is said that the world hears thunder where there is no sound, and beholds the autumn moon by a level lake. Should one's heart, upon reaching this place, grow calm as the still lake, then the bright moon dwells within oneself; and should one remain unmoved by praise or scorn, then every place becomes a level lake. Splendid scenes do not last, yet the level lake remains eternal—and this autumn moon may yet light the way for travelers to the ends of the earth.

Beauty fades, and shallow love never lasts. 
Only her love for herself is eternal, unaffected by time or the world. 
So Pearl will always, always love herself the most.

【下经·䷠】

䷠
遁：亨。小利贞。
彖曰：“遁亨”，遁而亨也。刚当位而应，与时行也。“小利贞”，浸而长也。遁之时义大矣哉！
《象》曰：天下有山，遁。君子以远小人，不恶而严。
初六：遁尾，厉，勿用有攸往。
《象》曰：“遁尾”之“厉”，不往何灾也？
六二：执之用黄牛之革，莫之胜说。
《象》曰：“执用黄牛”，固志也。
九三：系遁，有疾厉，畜臣妾吉。
《象》曰：“系遁”之“厉”，有疾惫也。“畜臣妾吉”，不可大事也。
九四：好遁，君子吉，小人否。
《象》曰：君子好遁，小人否也。
九五：嘉遁，贞吉。
《象》曰：“嘉遁，贞吉”，以正志也。
上九：肥遁，无不利。
《象》曰：“肥遁，无不利”，无所疑也。

en:
【Lower Canon·䷠】

䷠
Retreat: Success. Small and fitting to be steadfast.
The Commentary says: "Retreat succeeds," for in retreating there is success. The firm is in the proper position and responds, acting in accord with the times. "Small and fitting to be steadfast" means it gradually grows. Great indeed is the significance of the time of Retreat!
The Image says: Heaven below the Mountain: Retreat. The noble person thereby keeps distant from petty people, not with aversion but with dignity.
Initial Six: Retreating at the tail brings danger. Do not use this for any undertaking.
The Image says: The danger of "retreating at the tail" — if one does not go forth, what calamity is there?
Six in the Second: Holding fast with the hide of a Yellow Ox, none can loosen it.
The Image says: "Holding fast with the Yellow Ox" means firming the will.
Nine in the Third: Tied retreat brings illness and danger. Keeping servants and concubines is auspicious.
The Image says: The danger of "tied retreat" is the weariness of illness. "Keeping servants and concubines is auspicious" — one cannot undertake great matters.
Nine in the Fourth: Favorable retreat: the noble person is auspicious; the petty person is not.
The Image says: The noble person retreats favorably; the petty person does not.
Nine in the Fifth: Excellent retreat: steadfastness brings good fortune.
The Image says: "Excellent retreat, steadfastness brings good fortune" means rectifying the will.
Top Nine: Generous retreat: nothing is unfavorable.
The Image says: "Generous retreat, nothing is unfavorable" means there is no doubt.

Everyone speculated about the song's origins, and clues pointed to the Donghua gate. The taverns in the capital descended into chaos, but the Velvet Shade remained calm, capturing the hearts of guests with a song. Afterward, the investigators were never seen again, and commoners were intoxicated by the song. No one mentioned the song again.

zh:
西西是一只爱笑的小狗，对谁都会露出一副亲切和善的笑容，叫人们总会忘记当年它瘦骨嶙峋，一身渗血伤痕的可怜模样。
起初，西西很抗拒与人接触。只是它的抗拒与旁的小狗不同：它不会乱叫，不会咬人，只会尽可能缩进角落里，将头低低埋下，徒劳地将自己“藏”起来。
新主人十分怜惜西西，花了许多时间与耐心来陪伴它：拿走了西西临时住所周围所有可能让它感到恐惧的东西，为它轻轻清洁、处理伤势，又在它因恐惧而拒食时，一点点将炖得烂糊的食物一点点喂给它…… 终于，在冬日到来之前的那个清晨，西西主动缓步走到了刚刚推开房门的新主人面前，用脑袋轻轻地，不甚熟练地蹭了蹭新主人的衣摆。
尽管有着许多不好的经历，但在新主人的陪伴下逐渐走出阴霾的西西仍旧愿意去信任与亲近他人。
它总是那么热心肠，会帮弄掉钱袋的路人拾起钱袋，会为害怕虫蛇的孩童驱赶虫蛇，会主动凑近眼馋它那一身蓬松柔软毛发的陌生人，让他们能过一把手瘾…… 不过，在面对恶意时，它仍不会像很多威风的护卫犬一样挺身而出，而是会第一时间咬起想要守护之人的衣摆，快速逃离危险！
en:
Xixi is a dog who smiles. She gives everyone a warm, gentle grin, and it makes people forget the pitiful creature she once was, all bones and bleeding wounds.
At first, Xixi wanted nothing to do with people. But she didn't resist the way other dogs do. She never barked wildly, and she never bit. She would only curl herself as small as she could into a corner, her head low, trying futilely to hide.
Xixi's new owner loved her very much, and spent a great deal of time and patience in her company. Clearing away anything near her temporary shelter that might frighten her, gently cleaning and tending to her wounds, and when fear kept her from eating, feeding her food stewed soft, a little at a time... At last, on a morning before winter came, Xixi slowly walked on her own toward her new owner, who had just pushed open the door, and gently, clumsily nuzzled against the hem of his robe.
Despite all she had suffered, Xixi found her way out of the shadows under her new owner's care, and she is still willing to trust people and grow close to them.
She is always so warm-hearted. She picks up dropped coin bags for passersby, chases off bugs and snakes for frightened children, and even approaches strangers admiring her soft, fluffy coat so they can have their fill of petting... When faced with real malice, though, she wouldn't step forward the way a mighty guard dog would. She would take the hem of the one she means to protect in her teeth and bolt for safety!

en:
Preface
Do your customers finish their meals and leave without a word of praise? Do you envy the endless crowds at the tavern across the street?
Worry no more! This book teaches you 108 sure-fire ways to bring in customers. No special talent required. Just read, practice, and watch your guests weep with gratitude!
A first-rate waiter needs a quick tongue and a keen eye. Above all, though, you must know how to touch a customer's heart!
Today, I reveal every secret of this art. Follow my methods, and your guests will leave in tears, utterly devoted to your establishment.

First: A Little Culture
When showing customers your ingredients, don't stop at the ingredients.
Draw their attention to the reflections on the lake and the fish leaping beneath the moon.
Explain that only a fish this happy could become a meal that brings such joy. Once you've set the mood, recite a few lines of poetry. Your guests will be convinced they've entered a haven of culture and refinement. How could they fail to be impressed?

zh:
星占择日等数术在汉代社会生活中占有极为重要的地位。《汉书·艺文志》著录天文、历谱、五行、蓍龟、杂占、形法等数术类著作百九十家，二千五百八十二卷。虽然数目浩瀚，但其实远远不能囊括汉代数术类文献之全部。《艺文志》所载应是在精英知识分子群体中流传的数术类书籍，而非民间大众文化中的数术类图书，但《汉书·艺文志》中却不见《日书》踪影。由此可知，《日书》类书籍恐怕是民间对各种择日、杂占类技巧的整合，与精英分子的数术类书籍有关联但并不完全一致。甘肃汉简中也包含有不少数术类文献，且具备实用性的特点，其中以历谱、算术书和占卜类文献为多。
此简为《日书》类文献。主要内容与日忌有关，记某年内不宜杀六畜见血的日子。
en:
Astrology, the selection of auspicious dates, and other mystical arts were central to life in the Han Dynasty. The imperial bibliography in the Book of Han: Treatise on Literature lists a staggering 190 schools of thought and 2,582 scrolls dedicated to astronomy, the calendar, the Five Elements, and high divination. Yet, this massive collection only tells the story of the intellectual elite. Conspicuously missing from the imperial records is the Book of Days. Functioning much like a traditional farmer's almanac, the Book of Days was the everyday guide for the common people, a practical blend of lucky dates, daily superstitions, and folk magic. The Han Dynasty slips discovered in Gansu are full of these practical texts, giving us a rare, grounded look into the daily rituals and beliefs of ordinary citizens.
This specific bamboo slip is a surviving fragment from one of these Books of Days. It acts as an ancient calendar of taboos, listing the exact days of the year when it was strictly forbidden to shed blood or slaughter the "six domestic animals" (horses, cattle, sheep, pigs, dogs, and poultry).

zh:
天道不公，我取一二。此非行骗，乃为劫富。所得之财，自济当济之人。
聂浩轮，三十好几的人了，还爱干强买强卖的缺德事。前两天在长兴集，瞧上个老头的玉佩，想用十个子儿给黑了。老头不肯，结果当场就被他一顿打，玉佩也抢走了。
可见此人极要面子，对付他，就得当着他小弟的面，损他是个睁眼瞎，猜不中三仙归洞球落谁家，他肯定要来比划比划。等他一上桌……保管让他血本无归。
禄高阳，二十八，年纪不大，谱儿倒不小，专在街面上收保护费，哪个摊贩敢说个不字，他就叫人把人家吃饭的家伙全给砸了，断人活路。
这小子，激将不得，只能捧杀。找个大酒楼，当着所有人的面把他捧到天上去，再哄他开个局，让他露几手显摆显摆。就冲名声，他准应下来，到时候让他输几次……怕是他借钱也要继续往下猜。
熊备，三十来岁，就是个街溜子，滚刀肉，要钱不要命的主儿。为几个钱，他真敢当街掏刀子捅人。跟这种人不用废话，直接利诱就行。去他常去的赌坊，让空空儿赢几把大的给他看，等他上了钩，就来个狠的，到时候再把官府的人引来……让他牢底坐穿！
厉峯……
张博达……
王衙内……
……
en:
The world may be unjust, so I take what's owed. This isn't deceit—it's robbing the rich to help those in need. 
In his thirties, Nie Haolun is still up to no good—bullying, forcing trades, and strong-arming others. Just days ago at Crosswind Bazaar, he tried to swindle an old man's jade pendant for a mere ten coins. When the man refused, Nie beat him on the spot and snatched the pendant. 
He's a man obsessed with saving face. To handle him, bait him in front of his crew and mock his blindness—claim he can't handle the "Three to the Cave." He'll want to prove himself. Once he sits at the table, make sure he walks away empty-handed. 
Lu Gaoyang, only twenty-eight, is bold and arrogant. He runs protection rackets openly on the street, smashing pots and pans of any merchant who dares refuse him—cutting off their means to live. 
You can't provoke this kid with force; flattery is the only way. Take him to a grand tavern, heap praise on him in front of everyone, and coax him into a game where he can show off. With his pride, he won't resist. Once he's hooked, let him lose a few rounds... Soon enough, he'll be borrowing money and chasing debt. 
Xiong Bei is a ruthless street thug in his thirties—cold as a butcher and reckless to boot. He's quick to draw a knife over a few coins without hesitation. No use wasting time with him—simple temptation works best. Go to the gambling den he frequents; have Kongkong win big to catch his attention. Once he takes the bait, hit him hard and bring in the law... Let him rot behind bars where he belongs! 
Li Feng... 
Zhang Boda... 
Squireling Wang... 
...

……直到此地变成残垣，她辜负了太多的等待。
即使再冷，她也要孤身一人在彻骨寒心的时间里穿行。
她要回到过去，回到她错过的每一天。

en:
Time froze here.
Few people knew that what she feared most was the cold.
Perhaps she had known too much warmth in this life. Those who waited for her were always willing to leave a lantern burning; no matter how heavy the night dew grew, she never felt the chill.
...Until this place was reduced to ruins, and she failed too many of those who had waited.
No matter how cold it became, she had to travel alone through the bone-chilling flow of time.
She had to return to the past, to every day she had missed.
Amidst the shifting shadows, she seemed to catch glimpses of the people she could not let go of.
Oh, world, why can we not return to the very beginning?

zh:
阿藤讨厌在地面行走。那些碎石子硌着肉垫也就罢了，最可气的是，它一抬头只能看见人类的衣角，除非它豁出颜面仰躺在地上——可当它被迫袒露肚皮时，那个讨厌鬼偏不识好歹要来伸手乱揉。可别说，还、还挺舒服的。
这简直是奇耻大辱！它发誓，要比人还高、比葡萄藤还高、比房屋还高。晨露沾湿的藤条在爪下摇晃，却不妨碍它骄傲地俯视下方焦灼的人。这下自己终于不费吹灰之力就看到人的全身了！当然下场就是一脚踩空——它从藤上重重地摔了下来，被下面的人稳稳地伸手接住。
后来，阿藤学会了稳当地上藤。有一天藤下的人跟它说自己很快就会回来。可是等啊等、等啊等——它最开始在藤上等，然后在藤下等，后来又到了山路上等。再等不到，阿藤就要去别地找了。
en:
Vine hated walking on rough ground—the sharp stones hurt its paws. Worse, all it saw were human legs unless it lay back and exposed its belly, inviting unwanted rubs. Yet it found that comforting. 
Humiliated, Vine vowed to grow taller than humans, grapevines, and houses. Perched on dew-soaked vines, it proudly looked down below—until a slip sent it falling, caught safely by waiting hands. 
Afterward, Vine climbed cautiously. Then a voice promised to return, it waited—above, below, and along the path—until it realized it might have to move on if the person never came back.
